summary:
Solbound is a story-driven survival game where players lead a four-person crew through a 30-day mission on the Moon or Mars. Players recruit three companions from a pool of sixteen specialists. They then pack equipment within a 520 kg launch budget that also counts the crew’s own body mass. On the surface they balance oxygen, water, power, food and radiation shielding while dust storms, meteor showers, system failures and crew tensions force hard decisions. Every choice has a visible cost, and the goal is to bring everyone home.

The game responds to the challenge by letting students feel the consequences of engineering decisions in an off-Earth habitat. Solar storms in Solbound are not invented. Coronal mass ejections recorded in NASA’s DONKI database become radiation events in the mission, shown with their real dates, speeds and model forecasts. The game always labels which details come from science and which are gameplay assumptions.

This matters because space weather is one of the biggest risks to future crews, yet few people understand it. Solbound makes that risk tangible, runs in any browser, and is available in English and Turkish.
details:
What it does
Solbound is a browser-based survival game set on the Moon or Mars. Players create their own astronaut and pick three companions from sixteen candidates, each with different skills, personalities and body mass. Then they pack for launch within a 520 kg budget that includes the crew’s own weight and personal kits. After landing at one of eight real sites per destination, each with its own difficulty, they run a 30-day surface mission. Oxygen, water, power, food and radiation shielding must stay in balance. Dust storms, meteor showers, moonquakes, equipment failures and crew conflicts arrive as decision cards. Big events come with countdowns, so players can prepare. Every option has a visible cost. To win, players must book a return window, carry enough supplies for the trip home and get everyone back. At the end they receive a shareable recap of their mission.

How it works
Space weather in Solbound comes from real data. Coronal mass ejections from NASA’s DONKI database become radiation events in the game, and the game shows each one’s real date, speed and model-forecast arrival time. The game engine is deterministic and fully separate from the interface, so the same seed and the same NASA data always produce the same mission. Every event clearly labels which details are scientific facts and which are gameplay assumptions.

Benefits and impact
Solbound teaches the trade-offs of engineering decisions in an off-Earth habitat through experience rather than lectures. It turns space weather, an invisible and little-known risk to future crews, into something tangible. The game runs in any browser with no installation and is available in English and Turkish, so it can easily be used in classrooms.

Tools and technologies
TypeScript, React and Vite; Vitest for engine tests (66 passing); Playwright for automated end-to-end playthroughs; the NASA DONKI API, with a bundled offline snapshot as a fallback; and a GitHub Actions workflow prepared to refresh that snapshot. All artwork was drawn as original SVG. No special hardware was needed.

Creativity
Instead of a resource-management spreadsheet, Solbound tells a story through people. The crew talk to each other, react to the player’s choices and can be lost. Real solar storms make every mission connected to the actual Sun.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: sources are kept separate from game assumptions.
  • Two meaningfully different destinations: the Moon and Mars play differently.
  • Fairness: the deterministic engine makes the game testable and fair.
  • Accessibility: two languages, desktop and mobile layouts.
  • Clear disclaimer: this is an independent student project and not an official NASA product.
